article.title: A Fire Rescue Gift for My Child: A Father's Hope for Papua's Forests
article.description: A father's personal reflection on why Papua needs stronger fire and rescue services, the protection of its forests and Indigenous communities, and the right of Papuans to discuss their political future.
article.dek: A small Fire Rescue toy becomes a father's reflection on emergency services in Papua, forest fires, Papuan history, self-determination, and the future he hopes to leave his child.
article.intro: I want to give my child a small Fire Rescue toy. To a child, it may simply be a toy vehicle. To me, it is a reminder that Papua needs reliable firefighters and rescue services that can reach people when homes, public places, or forests are threatened by fire. Alongside it is a football booklet featuring Virgil van Dijk in the Netherlands colours—a small visual detail that leads me to reflect on Papua's complicated history with the Netherlands, its political future, and what I hope to pass on to my child.

sections.heading: A Small Gift, and a Real Need in Papua
paragraphs: There is a simple happiness in giving a child a gift. It does not have to be expensive or grand. Sometimes a small present can carry a meaning that lasts much longer than the moment it is opened.

I want to give my child a Fire Rescue toy. It represents the people who respond when others are in danger. In Papua, that image connects to a real public need: communities require firefighters and rescue teams that are properly equipped, trained, and able to reach emergencies quickly.

Fire is not limited to forests. Homes, markets, schools, workplaces, public buildings, and other places can also catch fire. When an emergency happens, every minute matters. A community needs functioning fire engines, protective equipment, water supplies, trained personnel, accessible fire stations, and clear ways to report an incident.

Papua's geography makes emergency response especially challenging. Some communities are far from urban centres; others face difficult terrain, limited road access, or narrow streets that can delay vehicles. In such circumstances, the distance to a fire station and the availability of suitable equipment can make a serious difference.

A fire and rescue service should not be measured only by the number of vehicles it owns. It should be measured by whether help can reach people, whether responders are trained and protected, and whether the service is prepared for the conditions of each community.

sections.heading: Why Papua Needs Stronger Fire and Rescue Services
paragraphs: Papua needs a stronger and more evenly distributed emergency response system. This means more than adding vehicles to a city fleet. It means maintaining equipment, training personnel, providing adequate water and protective gear, establishing strategically located stations, and supporting local communities with prevention education.

The needs of an urban neighbourhood are not always the same as those of a remote village. In some places, a conventional fire engine may be difficult to use. Local planning should therefore consider suitable vehicles, water access, communications, transport by land or water where necessary, and coordination with community responders.

Fire and rescue personnel may also be called upon to assist with evacuations and other emergencies within their training and authority. Their work deserves respect, investment, and reliable support. The safety of a person should not depend simply on whether that person lives close to a city centre.
I hope that one day people across Papua—whether in towns or remote communities—can have a fair chance of receiving timely help when fire or another emergency threatens their lives.

sections.heading: Fire Rescue and the Forests of Papua
paragraphs: The Fire Rescue toy also makes me think about forest and land fires. Papua's forests are not simply stands of trees. They are habitats for wildlife, sources of food and water, places connected to customary life, and part of the inheritance that Indigenous communities have protected across generations.

When forests burn, the damage reaches far beyond the trees. Fires can destroy habitats and vegetation, affect air quality, threaten gardens and food sources, and disrupt the daily lives of communities. Smoke can affect health, schooling, travel, and work. Some environmental losses cannot be repaired simply by planting a few new trees.

Forest fires require a response suited to the landscape. That can include early detection, field verification of reported hotspots, trained crews, suitable equipment, water and logistical support, coordination with local communities, and plans for areas that are difficult to reach. Prevention is just as important as suppression.

The causes of individual fires must be established through evidence. Dry conditions, human activity, land clearing, and other factors can contribute to fire risk, but no particular person or organisation should be blamed without a proper investigation. At the same time, authorities have a responsibility to monitor land-use change, enforce environmental laws, investigate suspected violations, and protect communities affected by fires.

I criticise development policies when they allow forests to be damaged, disregard Indigenous land rights, or put short-term economic interests ahead of people's safety and the environment. Development should not be judged only by investment figures or the amount of land opened. It should also be judged by whether people remain safe, customary rights are respected, and forests can continue to support future generations.

Indigenous communities are not obstacles to environmental protection. Their knowledge of forests, rivers, seasons, and local conditions should be respected and included in decisions. Papua needs prevention, accountability, and genuine partnership with the people who live closest to the land.

sections.heading: The Netherlands Booklet and Papua's History
paragraphs: The football booklet that comes with the toy features Virgil van Dijk wearing the Netherlands colours. I am not writing about his football achievements. In this story, the image is simply a visual reminder of the Netherlands and its historical relationship with Papua.

The Netherlands exercised colonial rule over western New Guinea. That history should not be romanticised or treated as though colonial rule was liberation. At the same time, a careful account of Papua's past must include the political developments among Papuans during the final years of Dutch administration, including the emergence of institutions and leaders who discussed the territory's future.

On 15 August 1962, Indonesia and the Netherlands signed the New York Agreement. The United Nations Temporary Executive Authority, known as UNTEA, took over the administration on 1 October 1962. The administration was transferred to Indonesia on 1 May 1963.

The agreement provided for an act of self-determination before the end of 1969. The process known as the Act of Free Choice, or Pepera, became the basis for the incorporation of Papua into Indonesia. Its implementation remains contested. Questions about representation, participation, and the freedom available to Papuans continue to be discussed in historical and political debates.

Papuans do not all hold the same political position. Some support integration with Indonesia, some seek changes within the Indonesian state, and others advocate independence. Those differences should be acknowledged honestly. But the dignity of Papuans and their right to express their views must be respected.

For me, discussing self-determination is a discussion about political voice, dignity, justice, and the ability of people to speak peacefully about their future. It should not be treated as hatred toward another people. The history of Papua deserves to be studied in full, including the voices of Papuans themselves.

sections.heading: A Father's Criticism and the Future of Papua
paragraphs: I love Papua not only because I was born here, but because this land holds people's lives, histories, cultures, and hopes. I want to see public institutions serve communities in practical ways: through education, healthcare, environmental protection, public safety, and emergency services that are ready when people need them.

What does development mean if a family cannot get help when its home catches fire? What does progress mean if forests are damaged and Indigenous communities lose the places that sustain their lives? Roads, buildings, and investment projects matter, but they cannot be the only measures of progress.

I criticise Indonesian government policies when they fail to protect Papuans, disregard customary rights, allow environmental damage to continue, or leave communities without adequate public services. Government responsibility should be visible in people's everyday safety and dignity, not only in announcements and project figures.

Papua should not be valued only for the natural resources that can be extracted from its land. It must also be valued through its people, cultures, forests, and the right of its communities to take part in decisions about their future.

sections.heading: What I Hope to Pass on to My Child
paragraphs: When I give my child the Fire Rescue toy, I want it to bring happiness. I also hope that, as my child grows, it will become a starting point for understanding the people who protect others in emergencies.

I want my child to know that protecting life means more than putting out a fire after it starts. It also means preventing fires, respecting the environment, helping neighbours, and supporting public services that can respond when people are in danger.

I want my child to learn Papua's history from different sources, to understand identity, and to ask thoughtful questions about justice and the future. I want knowledge rather than hatred, courage rather than fear, and respect for people whose political views may be different.

I do not know what Papua will look like when my child is grown. I hope it will be a safer place, with reliable emergency services, protected forests, respected Indigenous communities, and room for peaceful discussion about its future.

article.closing:
I may only be able to give my child a small Fire Rescue toy today. But I hope it carries a much larger message: Papua needs emergency services that can reach its people, forests that are protected, and public decisions that respect the dignity and rights of its communities.

I want my child to inherit knowledge, care for others, respect for nature, and the courage to seek the truth. Most of all, I hope my child can grow up in a Papua that is safer, fairer, and full of hope.

— Michael Gilroy Jitmau
